summary: Describes the policy, authorization and enforcement requirements for choosing which services get applied to a given OPES data flow. It focuses on who may decide which edge services act on traffic, and how those decisions are enforced.

eli5.summary: Who gets to decide which helpers touch your parcel, and how do we make sure the rules are followed? This document lists what is needed to answer that.

questions: who decides which edge services apply to traffic
what is a policy decision point
what is a policy enforcement point
what are the opes rule processing points
subtitle: What an OPES system must require so the right people decide which edge services touch which traffic.

tldr.problem: OPES services transform traffic between a data provider and a data consumer, so there must be clear rules about who may choose which services are applied, and a way to enforce them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits policy into a Rule Author, a Policy Decision Point that authenticates authors and compiles rules, and a Policy Enforcement Point in the data filter, and then sets requirements for interfaces, rules, authentication, authorization, integrity and privacy.
tldr.outcome: It gives requirements only, using MUST and SHOULD, and leaves rule formats and transport mechanisms out of scope.

today: RFC 3838 is an Informational RFC from August 2004 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It sits alongside the architecture in RFC 3835 and the threat analysis in RFC 3837.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
In the OPES architecture (RFC 3835), services run under a set of rules installed on the OPES processor. Rule evaluation can trigger a service on the processor or on a remote callout server. This RFC states the requirements for the policies that decide which services are applied to a message, if any.

The scope is limited to policies that say which services to call and with what parameters. Policies that dictate how the called services behave are not covered. The keywords MUST, SHOULD and so on follow RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: This document is about the rulebook for choosing helpers, not about how the helpers do their jobs.

sections.title: Policy Components
sections.content:
Policy is split into three parts: a Rule Author who provides rules, a Policy Decision Point (PDP) and a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP). The PDP is essentially a policy compiler. It MUST authenticate rule authors, verify that rules are within the author's authority, and be a component of the OPES Administration Authority. The PEP is the data filter, where OPES flow data is checked against compiled rules and the requested services are called.

The interface between rule authors and the PDP (the PDP Interface) MUST use the format resulting from this document's requirements. The PEP Interface can be internal to a vendor's processor, but MUST use a standard interface if the PDP and PEP are on different OPES processors.
sections.eli5: One person writes a rule, a checker makes sure they are allowed to write it, and a guard at the belt follows the checked rule.

sections.title: How the Enforcement Point Works
sections.content:
Rules MAY chain several services together, and implementations MUST pass information from one called service to the next. They MUST NOT prohibit re-evaluating a message to see whether another service should be called. Because an action may change message properties (for example, converting JPEG to GIF changes the content type), the data filter SHOULD act on matched rules before it evaluates later ones.

Any PEP or PDP MUST support four rule processing points: request handling when received from the data consumer application, request handling before forwarding to the data provider, response handling when received from the provider, and response handling when forwarding to the consumer.
sections.eli5: The guard looks at each parcel at four spots: when it arrives, before it goes on, when the answer comes back, and before it is handed over.

sections.title: Interface and Rule Requirements
sections.content:
Services MUST be specifiable in a location-independent way, so rule authors need not name a particular instance; the PEP MUST be able to resolve a generic name to a specific one, and a service description method such as WSDL MUST be present. Rule providers MUST be authenticated and authorized for their network role and MUST NOT specify rules outside their authority. Compiling rules from different sources MUST NOT lead to execution of conflicting rules, though resolving conflicts is out of scope.

Rule conditions MUST be matched against attribute values of the encapsulated protocol and environment variables. The rule system SHOULD allow unconditional rules, and actions MUST identify the service to run and pass any run-time parameters. Policy data elements such as user identity and profile MUST have agreed definitions across all OPES providers.
sections.eli5: Rules should say what kind of helper is needed, not which exact helper. Everyone has to agree what words in the rules mean.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
An OPES service provider MUST let all users request addition, deletion or blocking of services for their own traffic, prevent untrusted users from interfering with others, let users see their profiles, log profile activity for audit and follow a privacy policy. Users MUST be able to query the PDP to learn which rules apply to their traffic, and the PDP's identity for a user MUST be strictly mapped to the PEP's identity (for example an IP address).

Individuals who change their services MUST be authenticated, and the RFC says this SHOULD use strong authentication with a public key certificate. The PEP Interface MUST use a secure transport protocol. Each service MUST have a unique name cryptographically bound to the entity responsible for it. A "block all OPES" directive MUST be supported per user. Where an end user blocks a service that a trusted user wants applied, the end user SHOULD prevail unless there are security or legal reasons.
sections.eli5: Before anyone changes which helpers touch their parcels, they must prove who they are. And you should always be able to say no to helpers for your own parcels.

sections.title: Integrity, Encryption and Privacy
sections.content:
Because OPES services transform content, end-to-end cryptographic protection cannot be used. Where lesser protection is wanted, hop-by-hop protection is possible: the two ends of each hop MUST share a secret, which can differ between hops, and the secret MUST be unique for each requestor and responder pair. Encryption can be requested separately and applies to all processing points, including callout servers.

The PDP MUST have a privacy policy, and users MUST be able to prevent identity from being given to callout servers, prevent profile information from being shared, and prevent traffic from being sent to third-party callout servers or from particular sites from reaching callout servers. Third-party services MUST have a privacy policy and say how to access it.
sections.eli5: A sealed envelope cannot be changed by helpers, so each step of the trip gets its own lock. You can also tell the system not to share your name or your parcels with certain helpers.

layers.label: Rule Author
layers.detail: Provides the rules; talks to the PDP over the PDP Interface

layers.label: Policy Decision Point
layers.detail: Authenticates authors, validates and compiles rules

layers.label: Policy Enforcement Point
layers.detail: Data filter that evaluates traffic against compiled rules and calls services; reached over the PEP Interface
